title: Rotting Oranges
statement: A rectangular grid holds oranges. A cell is empty (0), holds a fresh orange (1), or holds a rotten orange (2). Every minute, each fresh orange that shares a side with a rotten orange (above, below, to the left or to the right) turns rotten, and all of these changes happen at the same moment. Find the number of minutes after which no fresh orange is left. If some fresh orange can never turn rotten, the answer is -1.
input_format: First line: R and C. Then R lines of C integers, each 0, 1 or 2.
output_format: One integer: the number of minutes, or -1.

examples.explain: The corner orange rots its two neighbours in minute 1, the next ones in minute 2, and the last orange rots in minute 4.
The orange in the bottom left corner is surrounded by empty cells, so the rot can never reach it.

idea: Think of the rot as spreading in waves. Put every rotten orange in a queue, then process the queue one wave at a time. Each wave is one minute. Count the fresh oranges so you know when you are done, and whether some are cut off.
naive: Simulating each minute by scanning the whole grid costs R times C work per minute. A long winding path of oranges needs about R times C divided by two minutes, so the total grows with the square of the grid size.
hints: Does the order in which rotten oranges act matter, or do they all act at the same moment?
All rotten oranges spread at once. What would one minute look like if you only looked at the oranges that just rotted?
Breadth-first search visits cells in waves. What should be in the queue before it starts?

complexity.time_why: Each cell enters the queue at most once and does four neighbour checks.
complexity.space_why: In the worst case the queue holds a large share of the grid, for example when most cells start rotten.

mistakes: Counting one extra minute for the last wave, which has nothing left to rot.
Marking an orange rotten when it leaves the queue instead of when it enters, so it can be queued more than once.
Reading the queue size inside the loop, so oranges from the next minute join the current one.

enforce.space_reason: A minute-by-minute simulation and the queue-based solution both use O(R * C) memory, so no input separates them by space. The quiz covers space instead.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the queue-based solution on an R by C grid?
quiz.explanation: Each cell enters the queue at most once and does four neighbour checks.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case extra space of the queue-based solution?
quiz.explanation: If most cells start rotten, the queue holds a large share of the grid.

quiz.q: Why does a queue give the right order here?
options: It sorts the cells by value
It visits cells in order of distance, so each wave is one minute
It stops a cell from being visited twice by itself
It uses less memory than a stack
quiz.explanation: First in, first out visits cells by increasing distance from the nearest rotten orange.

quiz.q: A fresh orange is walled in by empty cells. What should the function return?
options: It depends on the grid size
quiz.explanation: That orange can never rot, so the answer is -1.

quiz.q: Many starting points spread at the same speed. Which idea fits?
options: Depth-first search from each source in turn
quiz.explanation: Starting the search from all sources at once gives every cell its distance to the nearest source.

clarifications.answer: The grid is at most 1000 by 1000.
Yes. If there are no fresh oranges, the answer is 0.
No. Only up, down, left and right.
Yes. There can be any number of rotten oranges.
You may change the grid if you want to.

nudges: Ask yourself what should be in the queue before the first minute passes.
Process the queue one wave at a time. How do you know where one wave ends?

followup.question: The grid is too large to fit in memory. What would you change?
followup.discussion: Neighbouring cells differ in distance from the nearest rotten orange by at most one, so only the previous, current and next waves matter. Keep those three sets in memory and read the original cell values from disk on demand. Memory then depends on the size of a wave, not on the whole grid, at the cost of more disk reads.

edge_cases: A fresh orange walled in by empty cells
A single row or a single column

walkthrough.text: Walk the grid once. Every rotten orange goes into the queue, because they all start spreading at minute 0. Count the fresh oranges so we know when we are done and whether some are left behind.
dx and dy list the four moves: down, up, right and left. Looping d from 0 to 3 visits every neighbour without writing the same code four times.

One pass of this loop is one minute. It runs while the queue still has oranges that can spread and at least one fresh orange remains. Checking the fresh count here stops the clock the moment the last orange rots, so no empty extra minute is counted.
q.size() is read once, before any pushes. That many oranges were rotten at the start of this minute. Oranges pushed during the loop can only rot others next minute, so they wait for the next pass.

Pop an orange and look at its four neighbours. Skip anything outside the grid or not fresh. A fresh neighbour rots immediately, the fresh count drops, and it joins the queue. Marking it when it is queued means no orange is ever queued twice.
The whole level is finished, so one minute has passed.
If the fresh count reached zero, minutes is the answer. If the queue ran dry while fresh oranges remain, empty cells cut them off from the rot, so return -1.
